issues.legal_issue: Consent by sapindas to a widow’s adoption implies that the adoption is considered desirable for spiritual purposes, so the widow’s motive need not be independently examined.
material_facts: The widow adopted without authority from her deceased husband and obtained the consent of two male sapindas.
Letters seeking consent and the adoption deed stated that the adoption was intended to secure the performance of religious ceremonies and spiritual benefit for the deceased husband and his ancestors.
The evidence showed that the consenting sapindas had no personal motive in giving consent.
Although the widow also anticipated material benefit from the adoption, the evidence showed that spiritual considerations were among her reasons.
issues.conclusion: The sapindas’ consent implied that the adoption was considered desirable for spiritual and religious purposes; the widow’s motive did not require separate inquiry, and the consent supported the adoption.
issues.legal_principle: Under the principles stated in V.T.S. Chandrasekhara Mudaliar v. Kulandai Velu Mudaliar, the consent of sapindas protects against a capricious adoption and is an assurance of bona fide performance of religious duty. Consent itself implies that the adoption was considered desirable for spiritual purposes; it is when consent is refused that the justification for the refusal must be examined. Consent given for the sapinda’s own personal motives would not validate an adoption.

predicates.sapindas_consented: Sapindas whose consent was sought gave consent to the adoption.

issues.definition: When a widow adopts without her deceased husband’s authority and sapindas consent, the widow’s motive need not be independently examined.

issues.legal_issue: The consent of a majority of the equally near male sapindas is sufficient to satisfy the requirement that a widow consult the nearest sapindas before adopting.
material_facts: Three male sapindas were equally near to the deceased husband.
The consent of two of them was established, while the third sapinda’s consent was not established.
The widow had adopted without authority from her deceased husband.
issues.conclusion: The consent of two out of the three equally near sapindas was sufficient to satisfy the consultation requirement and support the adoption.
issues.legal_principle: In applying the Hindu-law requirement that a widow without her deceased husband’s authority consult the nearest sapindas, the Court held that the consent of the majority of equally near sapindas is sufficient; the consent of every such sapinda is not essential.

predicates.majority_of_equally_near_sapindas_consen: More than half of the equally near sapindas whose consultation was required consented to the adoption.

issues.definition: When a widow adopts without her deceased husband’s authority, consent from a majority of the equally near sapindas satisfies the consultation requirement.

issues.legal_issue: A female sapinda is not required to consent to a widow’s adoption, even if she is nearer in degree than the male sapindas consulted.
material_facts: The widow adopted without authority from her deceased husband.
The deceased husband’s grandmother, a female sapinda nearer in degree than the consenting male sapindas, was alive when the adoption occurred.
The grandmother’s consent was not obtained.
The adoption had the consent of male sapindas.
issues.conclusion: The grandmother’s consent was not required to validate the adoption; the relevant consent was that of male sapindas.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the Hindu-law rationale that a widow’s need for sapinda consent arises from the law’s view that women cannot exercise independent judgment in this matter; a woman regarded as needing such consent herself is not a competent adviser whose consent must be obtained by another widow. The Court relied on V.T.S. Chandrasekhara Mudaliar v. Kulandai Velu Mudaliar and the Privy Council decisions in The Collector of Madura v. Mootoo Ramalinga Sethupatty, Veera Basavaraju v. Balasurya Prasada Rao, and Ghanta China Ramasubbayya v. Maparthi Chenchuramayya, which interpreted the relevant references to kindred as referring to male agnates. It disapproved contrary observations in Rajah Damara Kumara Venkatappa Nayanim Bahadur Varu v. Damara Renga Rao and Maharajah Kolhapur v. S. Sundaram Ayyar.
